# Experiences

## DOA and CRM Systems
- Organization: Smart Shift Solutions
- Role: Fullstack
- Type: Web Development
- Period: May – Jul 2026
- Article: https://medium.com/@BadLuckZ/what-10-weeks-as-a-fullstack-dev-qa-intern-taught-me-about-myself-at-smart-shift-solutions-482f88f2cd4b

### Information
This was my 10-week internship at Smart Shift Solutions (SSS) as a Fullstack Developer Intern.
I worked here from May 18 to July 31, 2026, as part of my university's Engineering Practice course.

Before my first day, I was given a one-week pretest project to fix bugs and add features, which doubled as a soft onboarding to the company's code style, tech stack, and folder structure. After receiving detailed feedback on it, I started working on two of the company's real, in-production systems:
1. DOA (Delegation of Authority) - a system that defines an approval hierarchy, where a higher-authority approver can decide out of order without waiting on approvers before them.
2. CRM (Customer Relationship Management) - a system supporting the end-to-end property sales workflow, covering reservations, approvals, contracts, payments, and document generation, which relies on DOA's approval decisions to move documents forward.
In week 2, I asked to try the QA role and ended up staying on that path for the rest of the internship. As QA, I worked from feature requirement slides and a detailed Test Script Sheet, covering:
1. Manual Testing through the real UI, filing new issues with clear pass/fail test steps whenever I found a bug.
2. Automated Testing with Playwright to guard against regressions on features that already worked.

### What I learned
There are 2 key things I learned during this internship.

1. Writing good code isn't enough without understanding the business domain.
Both as a Fullstack Developer fixing features and, even more so, as QA, I couldn't judge whether a feature actually matched what the business needed - or whether it still had bugs - without understanding the domain and the requirements behind it. This mattered even more since every flow touched money and customer permissions.

2. Thinking like QA changed how I write code as a developer.
My mindset shifted from "does this feature work correctly" to "where could this break." Bringing that habit back to Fullstack work made me more deliberate about planning test cases and handling edge cases properly, instead of just the happy path.

### Contribution
My work during this internship covered both QA and Fullstack Development on the DOA and CRM systems.

1. As a Fullstack Developer, I developed and maintained both frontend and backend features across DOA and CRM, picking up issues from the team's Working Sheet and fixing bugs reported through QA, with my work reviewed by my mentor.

2. As QA, I studied feature requirements and edge cases across the CRM's reservation, approval, contract, payment, and document generation flows, then wrote and ran manual test cases through the UI, filing issues with clear reproduction steps for any bugs found.

3. I wrote test documentation in the team's Test Script Sheet and built automated regression tests with Playwright to make sure previously working features stayed working as the system kept changing.

## Chula Openhouse 2026
- Organization: ISD, Chulalongkorn University
- Role: Frontend
- Type: Web Development
- Period: Jan – Apr 2026

### Information
This is the project from ISD (Information System Development), Chulalongkorn University.
This project started in January 2026 and finished in April 2026.

This project is about building a website that helps people register for Chulalongkorn University's Open House 2026, shares information from each faculty in the university, and includes a minigame called Missing Pieces where people can collect and exchange pieces to connect with others.

This project contributes to many parts.
1. Landing Page which is the first page. It includes announcement popups, promotional images from each faculty, a space for the university’s live streams, FAQs, Sponsors and more.
2. Register Page where users can register and log in to the system via Google Account.
3. Ticket Page which displays the user's information, allows users to register, and provides access to the evaluation form.
4. Faculty Page which shows each faculty's detail.
5. Workshop Page which shows workshops from each faculty.
6. Merchandise Page which shows official event merchandise and allows users to view product details and purchase information.
7. Missing Pieces Page which is the minigame of this website. Users can enter codes to exchange faculty pieces with friends and collect all 20 faculties. The page also includes personal statistics and allows users to share their collected pieces and overall progress with others.
Furthermore, there is a Staff Section that can only be accessed by registered staff members of the event to scan participants' QR codes for check-in.

Lastly, there is a Evaluation form to collect feedback from participants, with a certificate provided for high school users in return.

### What I learned
There are 2 things I can learn by participating in this project.

1. Taking the role of Senior Frontend Developer in a large-scale project.
This was my first time acting as a Senior Frontend Developer in a project that served over 50,000 users. I was responsible for planning the frontend feature set, dividing tasks among team members, reviewing code, and ensuring overall progress. It taught me how to think beyond just writing code - I had to consider the team's workflow, code consistency, and the impact of every decision on a system used by a large number of real users.

2. Building an automated certificate delivery system from scratch.
This was my first time independently building a standalone Python script outside of the main project. I learned how to generate personalized certificates by overlaying user data onto an image template, convert them into the proper format, and send them to thousands of recipients via email automatically. It gave me a broader perspective on how a complete system works end-to-end, not just the frontend side.

### Contribution
The parts I contributed to this project are as follows...

1. As a Senior Frontend Developer in a project serving over 50,000 users, I planned the overall frontend feature set, defined workflows for each section, and divided tasks among frontend team members while tracking progress throughout the development period.

2. I built a Base Component Library using React to ensure consistency across the project, making it easier for team members to build new features quickly and maintain a unified UI standard.

3. I was primarily responsible for the Missing Pieces minigame, including the page displaying each user's collected faculty pieces and the flow for entering codes to receive pieces from other participants.

4. I built the Faculty and Workshop pages to display detailed information about each faculty and their available workshops.

5. I developed the Evaluation Form page for collecting feedback from participants, and handled various detail improvements across other pages throughout the project.

6. I independently built a Certificate Sender system using Python, which automatically generates personalized certificates from a template and sends them to participants via email based on data from a CSV file. [Click](https://github.com/BadLuckZ/Project-Certificate-Sender) to view.

## CUCM Reward 2025
- Organization: ISD, Chulalongkorn University
- Role: Frontend
- Type: Web Development
- Period: Oct – Dec 2025

### Information
This is the project from ISD (Information System Development), Chulalongkorn University.
This project started in October 2025 and finished in December 2025.

This project is about building a reward-based web application for CUCM (Chula Chiangmai) Camp 2025, designed to encourage interaction between participants and staff through gifting, coin transactions, and event-based activities.

The system supports four roles: Participant, Staff, Moderator, and Admin. Each role has clearly defined permissions and access scopes to ensure proper control, fairness, and system stability.

Participants and staff can log in using a username and a 6-digit PIN. After logging in, users can answer a one-time secret question, which is later used as a validation mechanism for sending gifts between users. This answer can only be reset by an Admin.

The core features for Participant and Staff include:
1. Viewing personal information such as name, nickname, and school.
2. Sending gifts to other users by correctly answering the recipient’s secret question. Each user has a limited number of gift attempts per hour and cannot send gifts to the same person more than once per reset cycle.
3. Receiving coins from gifts and redeeming event codes to earn additional coins.
4. Using coins to support the central staff team or purchase tickets for prize draws.
5. Viewing transaction history including coin earnings, coin usage, and gifting records.
6. Competing on a leaderboard that can be filtered by role or viewed overall.
For Moderator, the system provides tools to create events and manage active redeem codes for participants.

And for Admin, the system includes advanced management features such as toggling system access by role, resetting user secret answers, adjusting coin balances, configuring ticket prices, managing events, and exporting ticket purchase data in CSV format for prize drawing.

### What I learned
There are 3 key takeaways I gained from participating in this project.

1. Taking the role of Senior Frontend Developer in a real project.
This was my first time acting as a Senior Frontend Developer, where I was responsible for planning frontend features, dividing tasks among team members, and ensuring overall progress.

2. Managing code quality and team collaboration.
I regularly reviewed pull requests, checked code consistency, verified feature correctness, and merged code to ensure that all parts worked together smoothly within the system.

3. Designing frontend architecture for complex business logic.
I gained experience in structuring frontend logic to support real-world constraints such as role-based permissions, limited actions, cooldown resets, and one-time access flows.

### Contribution
The parts I contributed to this project are as follows.

1. As a Senior Frontend Developer, I planned the overall frontend feature set, defined workflows for each user role, and divided tasks among frontend team members while tracking progress throughout the development period.

2. I was responsible for Participant and Staff features, including dashboards, gifting workflow, redeem code flow, coin usage, ticket purchasing, transaction history, and leaderboard logic.

3. I reviewed, tested, and merged frontend code from team members, ensuring consistency in coding style, correctness of logic, and smooth integration with backend APIs.

4. I implemented the authentication flow using username and 6-digit PIN, including role-based access control and post-login redirection.

## CUNEX Quick Attend
- Organization: CUNEX, Chulalongkorn University
- Role: Fullstack
- Type: Web Development
- Period: Aug 2025 – Jul 2026
- Demo: https://quickattend.cunex.club

### Information
This project was from CUNEX, Chulalongkorn University.
I worked on this project from August 2025 to July 2026.

This project involves developing a website integrated with CUNEX Authentication - a centralized platform for managing and registering student activities and events at Chulalongkorn University, implementing both frontend and backend features.

The website supports multiple user roles and provides the following main features:
1. Activity History where users can view their past activity participation records.
2. Activity Discovery where users can browse available activities and events to join as a participant.
3. Event Creation, Editing, and Deletion where users can create new events, becoming the Owner of that event, and manage its details afterward.
4. Role-Based Access Control where Owners can assign Managers and Staff to their event, each with different permissions for managing and operating it.
5. QR Code-Based Attendee Registration which allows Staff, Manager, and Owner roles to scan participants' QR codes for attendee registration and check-in.
6. CUNEX Authentication where users log in using their CUNEX university account for secure and unified access to the platform.
7. Analytics Dashboard providing Staff, Manager, and Owner roles with insights into attendance numbers, check-in times, and attendee demographics by faculty.

### What I learned
There are 3 things I can learn by participating in this project.

1. This was my first time working on a production app used by real university students.
Working on this website gave me experience shipping features that are actively used by Chulalongkorn University students. I had to be more careful about edge cases, data consistency, and user experience compared to project-based work.

2. I gained experience implementing role-based functionality in a complex system.
The website has distinct permission levels for Participant, Staff, Manager, and Owner. Building UI and logic that adapts cleanly to each role taught me how to structure role-based access in a maintainable and scalable way.

3. I learned how to integrate QR code scanning into a real-world workflow.
Implementing QR code scanning for event check-in taught me how to bridge hardware input (camera) with backend registration logic, and how to handle scanning edge cases such as invalid codes or duplicate scans.

### Contribution
The parts I contributed to this project are as follows...

1. I implemented CUNEX-based authentication, allowing users to log in with their university account and access the website with the appropriate role and permissions.

2. I built the Activity History feature, enabling users to track their past participation records in a clear and organized view.

3. I developed the Activity Discovery section where users can browse and join available activities and events as a participant.

4. I worked on Event Creation, Editing, and Deletion, including the role-based access control that lets Owners assign Managers and Staff with different permissions on their event.

5. I implemented the QR code-based attendee registration functionality for event check-in, allowing Staff, Manager, and Owner roles to scan participants' QR codes and register their attendance.

6. I built the Analytics Dashboard, giving Staff, Manager, and Owner roles insights into attendance numbers, check-in times, and attendee demographics by faculty.

# Projects

## PromptPay QR Split
- Role: Fullstack
- Type: Web Development
- Period: Jun 2026 – Present
- GitHub: https://github.com/BadLuckZ/Project-PromptPay-QR-Split.git
- Demo: https://www.pqrsplit.com/
- Document: https://thanagorn.com/assets/pdf/pqr_split.pdf

### Information
This is my personal project called PromptPay QR Split.
This project started in June 2026.

I built this to solve a problem I kept running into with friends: after eating out together, I'm often busy and need to leave before everyone finishes, so I can't stick around to split the bill and collect cash or transfers from each person. This app lets anyone create a bill, add items and the people sharing them, and the system automatically calculates each person's share and generates a personal PromptPay QR code for them, so everyone can pay on their own time, whether or not the bill creator is still there.

This project is built with Next.js and Supabase, and contains key features such as Google Sign-in, Bill Creation with itemized splitting, Per-member PromptPay QR Generation, and Payment Status Tracking.

### What I learned
There are 3 things I can learn by doing this project

1. I learned how to build with the Next.js App Router alongside Supabase Auth and RLS.
I practiced server-side auth with `@supabase/ssr`, protecting routes, and designing row-level security policies so that each member can only see and pay their own share of a bill.

2. I got hands-on experience with the PromptPay QR payload spec.
I learned how to generate a valid EMVCo-based PromptPay QR payload per person and per amount, and render it as a scannable QR code on the fly.

3. I practiced designing a product around a real, personal pain point.
Since I was solving my own problem, I had to think carefully about the actual flow of splitting a bill with friends and make sure people could pay independently without needing to be in the same place at the same time.

### Contribution
Since this is my personal project, it means I have built everything in this project by myself.

## Buriram Constituency 1 Election Analysis 2026
- Role: Data Analyst
- Type: Data
- Period: Apr – May 2026
- GitHub: https://github.com/polar-bear-cu/dsde-buriram-1
- Demo: https://polar-bear-cu-dsde-buriram-1.streamlit.app/
- Document: https://thanagorn.com/assets/pdf/buriram_1_election_2026.pdf

### Information
This is my group project (4 members) called Buriram Constituency 1 Election Analysis.
This project started in April 2026 and it took 1 month to complete this analysis.

This project analyzes the 2026 Thai general election results for Buriram Constituency 1 by extracting data from official Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) PDF documents using OCR technology, then validating, cleaning, and visualizing the data to uncover voting patterns and candidate performance insights across all polling stations.

This project is built by Python and contains many key features such as OCR (Optical Character Recognition) powered by Typhoon, Data Validation, Data Analysis, Error Analysis, and an interactive Dashboard & Visualization.

### What I learned
There are 4 things I can learn by doing this project

1. I've learned how to extract structured data from real-world government documents using OCR.
I practiced using Typhoon, an LLM-based OCR engine, to extract election result tables from scanned ECT PDF documents. It was more challenging than I expected because the documents were inconsistent and noisy, so I had to handle many edge cases throughout the pipeline.

2. I got better at designing data validation and cleaning systems.
After extracting the data, I learned how to write validation rules to detect and correct OCR errors such as misread numbers, missing values, and formatting inconsistencies. This helped me understand how important data quality is before doing any analysis.

3. This project gave me a chance to practice real data analysis and error analysis.
I analyzed election results to identify voting patterns and candidate performance across polling stations. At the same time, I performed error analysis to measure OCR accuracy, which helped me understand how to evaluate the quality of an entire data pipeline.

4. I learned how to present data clearly through dashboards and visualizations.
I got to build an interactive dashboard to communicate complex election data in a way that is easy to understand. This improved my ability to think about how to present data meaningfully to different audiences.

### Contribution
My main responsibility covered the OCR pipeline and data validation parts of the project.

1. OCR Pipeline - Set up and configured the Typhoon-based OCR engine to extract election result tables from scanned ECT PDF documents, and handled preprocessing to improve extraction accuracy.

2. Data Validation - Designed and implemented validation rules to detect and correct errors in the OCR output, ensuring the data was accurate and consistent before passing it to the analysis stage.

3. Error Analysis - Measured OCR accuracy by comparing extracted data against reference values, identified common error patterns, and summarized findings to evaluate overall pipeline quality.

There are also areas where players can purchase new perks and upgrade existing perks to become stronger.

### What I learned
There are 2 things I can learn by doing this project

1. I’ve learned the challenges and hardships of game development.
I’ve always had questions about game development-for example, why do so many games I’ve played have bugs? Why aren’t they thoroughly tested before release? However, after working on this project with my friend, I understood why these situations happen. We tried to play our game as much as we can to solve the bugs inside the project and when our time to present the project came, it still had bugs in our project.

2. This is my first chance to code with my friend. I thought it wouldn't be that hard but it's not like that.
Although our communication went well, many functions we wanted to code were harder than we thought due to our lack of experience and knowledge. So we decided to code the main features first such as movement systems and animations. When we had some time, we learned how to code things we wanted and applied to our projects. That situation improves our coding skills.

### Contribution
The parts I contributed to this project are as follows...

1. Player Movement
I coded the basic movement system for the player (left-right movement) and setting up the camera border to follow the player's position dynamically.

2. Damage Calculation
I designed the system for calculating various types of damage for both the player and monsters. This allows for a variety of damage outputs, with each attack producing different damage values.

3. Perk System
I implemented the abilities of different perks, as well as the systems for purchasing and upgrading them.

4. SFX
I was responsible for selecting the music and sound effects used throughout the game.
Additionally, I also assisted my partner in some aspects of this project. For example, I contributed to defining the stats for both the player and monsters, designing and creating various in-game scenes, and writing this project's documentation.
